case_name: Thomas v Saskatchewan Indian Gaming Authority Inc.
text:
Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan

Docket: CACV3844

Citation:
Thomas v Saskatchewan
Indian Gaming Authority Inc.
, 2021 SKCA 164

Date: 2021-12-15

Between:

Ian Edgar Thomas

Appellant

(Plaintiff)

And

Saskatchewan Indian Gaming
Authority Inc.

Respondent

(Defendant)

Before:

Schwann,
Leurer and Kalmakoff JJ.A.

Disposition:

Appeal
dismissed

Written reasons by:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Kalmakoff

In concurrence:

The Honourable Madam Justice Schwann

The Honourable Mr. Justice Leurer

On appeal from:

QBG
1833 of 2018, Saskatoon

Appeal heard:

November 4, 2021

Counsel:

Davin
R. Burlingham for the Appellant

Robert J. Frost-Hinz for the Respondent

Kalmakoff J.A.

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Ian Thomas worked for Saskatchewan Indian Gaming
Authority Inc. [SIGA] for more than eight years. In October of 2018, SIGA
terminated his employment without notice. He then sued SIGA for wrongful
dismissal, seeking pay in lieu of an appropriate notice period, and aggravated
damages in relation to SIGA’s conduct in the course of the dismissal. The
matter proceeded to trial in the Court of Queen’s Bench. The trial judge dismissed
Mr. Thomas’ claim, holding that SIGA had just cause to dismiss him, and that it
had not acted unfairly or in bad faith in doing so (
Thomas v Saskatchewan
Indian Gaming Authority Inc.
(12 May 2021) Saskatoon, QBG 1833/2018
(Sask QB) [
Trial Decision
]).

[
2
]

Mr. Thomas appeals against the
Trial Decision
.

He asserts that the trial judge made several legal and factual errors in
reaching the conclusions that he did. Mr. Thomas invites this Court to set
aside the
Trial Decision
, find that he was dismissed without just cause,
determine an appropriate notice period, and award damages.

[
3
]

For the reasons that follow, I would dismiss the
appeal.

II.

BACKGROUND

[
4
]

Mr. Thomas began working for SIGA in August of
2010. From early 2011 until his employment was terminated, he held the position
of procurement process support officer.

[
5
]

In the late summer of 2018, Mr. Thomas applied
for promotion to a management position in the procurement process department. He
was one of three candidates short-listed for the position.

[
6
]

On October 10, 2018, Mr. Thomas met with Martin
Hryniuk, SIGA’s director of procurement, to discuss training opportunities. During
the meeting, Mr. Thomas inquired as to whether a decision had been made about
the position he had applied for. Mr. Hryniuk advised Mr. Thomas that the
position had been awarded to another candidate, a woman.

[
7
]

Upon being informed of this, Mr. Thomas became
angry and aggressive. He accused Mr. Hryniuk of being a racist who did not
support the advancement of Indigenous men. He said words to the effect that he
would have had a better chance of being promoted if he had “cut his own balls
off”. Another supervisor, Herman Bugler, was called into the meeting by Mr.
Hryniuk. Mr. Thomas continued with his aggressive actions and tone after Mr.
Bugler entered the room. He leaned in towards Mr. Hryniuk and shook his finger
at him. He called the explanations given by Mr. Hryniuk for awarding the
promotion to another candidate “bullshit”. By the time Mr. Thomas left the
meeting, Mr. Hryniuk was quite shaken up, to the point that he drove around
aimlessly after leaving work, for fear that Mr. Thomas may come to his home.

[
8
]

Mr. Hryniuk filed a complaint with SIGA’s
Employee Relations Department [ERD]. The ERD investigated the matter. On
October 15, 2018, Mr. Thomas was placed on leave and instructed by SIGA not to
communicate with other employees pending the conclusion of the investigation.
On his way out of the building, after having just received this instruction,
Mr. Thomas encountered two other SIGA employees. He volunteered to them that he
had been placed on leave and told them it was because he had “told [Mr. Hryniuk]
how he really felt”. Mr. Thomas also contacted another SIGA employee the next
day, by telephone and text message. In those conversations, he referenced the
investigation and asked the other employee to download certain SIGA tender
templates and e-mail them to him.

[
9
]

On October 22, 2018, SIGA advised Mr. Thomas, by
way of a letter, that his employment would be immediately terminated, with
cause. The letter was co-written by Mr. Hryniuk and read, in part, as follows:

The decision has been
made after a thorough assessment of your conduct which has breached SIGA’s
Employee Code of Conduct Policy A04-601, and SIGA’s Anti-Harassment &
Workplace Violence Policy A04-611. In addition to breaching these policies, you
have also violated the expectations that SIGA has towards yourself in the
position of Procurement Process-Support Officer. The following is an outline of
the findings:

Conduct and
Behavior

Policy Violation:
Employee Code of Conduct A04-601

•

On October 10, 2018 you were called into a
meeting at approximately 4:30 p.m.. During this meeting … you continued to
question me with respect to the recent employment competition with which you
participated in.

•

You were advised that you were unsuccessful in
this competition, where you immediately began to show frustration, anger, and
resentment towards me in the position of Director of Procurement. During this
altercation you belittled my position within the department, you antagonized me
with respect to the decision that was made, you uttered threats to me, and you
placed me in a very awkward position.

•

The inappropriate comments that were made during
this altercation were a direct violation to SIGA’s Employee Code of Conduct
Policy, and SIGA’s Anti-Harassment Policy. Your comments and demeanour were
unprofessional and not in-line with what SIGA values in each employee.

…

[
10
]

The letter also stated that Mr. Thomas had breached
SIGA’s directions regarding communication with other employees and
confidentiality respecting the investigation, and that he had requested SIGA
property from a colleague while on administrative leave, which “placed this
employee in an extremely difficult position, questioning your motives towards
the employee and the organization”.

[
11
]

Mr. Thomas appealed the termination to SIGA’s
Senior Vice-President of Finance and Administration. His appeal was
unsuccessful; the termination was upheld.

[
12
]

Mr. Thomas filed a statement of claim with the
Court of Queen’s Bench on November 19, 2018. In it, he alleged that his
employment had been terminated without just cause. He sought to recover the
wages he would have earned during the appropriate notice period.

[
13
]

Mr. Thomas also claimed aggravated damages on
the basis that SIGA had “engaged in conduct during the course of the dismissal
that was unfair and in bad faith by being untruthful, misleading and unduly
insensitive”, which had caused him to “suffer mental distress, psychological
harm, and damage to his reputation”. Mr. Thomas based this claim on two
allegations: (i) that SIGA had falsely accused him of threatening, belittling
and intimidating a supervisor; and (ii) that SIGA had sent out a public notice
of his termination before the end of the period during which he could appeal
the decision.

[
14
]

SIGA defended the claim on the basis that it had
just cause to immediately terminate Mr. Thomas’ employment, on three
grounds: (i) multiple breaches of employment policies; (ii) breaches of the
common law duties of confidentiality and good faith (i.e., communicating with
other employees about the investigation and attempting to acquire SIGA property
from one of them); and (iii) harassment and insubordination towards a
supervisor.

[
15
]

The action proceeded to trial in the Court of
Queen’s Bench. As noted above, the trial judge dismissed Mr. Thomas’ claim,
finding that SIGA had just cause to terminate his employment, based on his
conduct during the October 10, 2018, meeting with Mr. Hryniuk. In that respect,
the trial judge wrote:

[32]      I return,
then, to a consideration of whether Mr. Thomas, during the meeting, “engaged in
misconduct that is incompatible with the fundamental terms of the employment
relationship”. I conclude that he did.

[33]      I find that
Mr. Thomas became angry and aggressive. He elevated the tension in the room to
the point where Mr. Hryniuk, his supervisor, felt threatened. As pleaded by
SIGA, he directed frustration, anger and resentment towards his supervisor, Mr.
Hryniuk. He belittled Mr. Hryniuk, attacking him on a point (dealing with First
Nations men) of fundamental significance to SIGA (as a First Nations
organization) and to Mr. Hryniuk (as a white person working in a First Nations
organization). Overall, he was insubordinate to Mr. Hryniuk.

[34]      The
employer-employee relationship could not continue after Mr. Thomas engaged in
this conduct. The relationship had been irretrievably severed. The relationship
requires a fundamental trust between employer and employee, and a capacity to
work together. Mr. Thomas' conduct destroyed both that fundamental trust and
the capacity to work together. Mr. Hryniuk cannot work with Mr. Thomas, and it
is not realistic or reasonable to think that any other person in a supervisory
or management role with SIGA could do so. Effectively, Mr. Hryniuk was
aggressive and insubordinate not only to Mr. Hryniuk but also to SIGA itself
and its managers and supervisors.

[35]      Despite Mr.
Thomas' many years of service with SIGA, and despite SIGA's
previously-expressed hope that with continued training Mr. Thomas would advance
within the organization, his conduct during the meeting struck at the heart of
the employment relationship.

[36]      Furthermore,
with that conduct Mr. Thomas breached SIGA policies that he knew applied to
him. He has acknowledged that he was bound to follow the policies, and that he
had been aware of the content and effect of the policies. In particular, his
conduct during the meeting breached:

(a) the Employee
Code of Conduct policy, in that he did not treat Mr. Hryniuk and Mr. Bugler
with dignity and respect, and he did not conduct himself appropriately and
professionally; and

(b) the
Anti-Harassment & Workplace Violence policy, in that he engaged in
disruptive behaviour towards Mr. Hryniuk.

[37]      SIGA had
just cause to dismiss Mr. Thomas without notice or pay in lieu thereof.

[
16
]

The trial judge also concluded that Mr. Thomas
had breached SIGA’s instruction not to communicate with other employees during
the course of the investigation and that he had breached the Employee Code of
Conduct regarding confidentiality by trying to obtain proprietary documents
belonging to SIGA for the use of another organization. He found that neither of
these two misdeeds were cause for dismissal on their own but, when taken
together with Mr. Thomas’ conduct in the October 10, 2018, meeting, they supported
the conclusion that SIGA had just cause for dismissal, because “[t]he
irreparable rift in the employer-employee relationship was made even deeper by
Mr. Thomas having breached the direction and by Mr. Thomas having requested the
tender documents” (
Trial Decision
,

at para 51).

[
17
]

The trial judge also considered and dismissed
Mr. Thomas’ claim for aggravated damages. He found that nothing in the manner
in which SIGA had dealt with Mr. Thomas could be described as being unfair or
in bad faith and that “[n]othing that it did is demonstrated to have been
untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive” and, moreover, the evidence did
not establish that the loss and upset that Mr. Thomas experienced had resulted
from the manner of the dismissal as opposed to the fact of the dismissal (
Trial
Decision
at paras 55–56).

III.

THE ISSUES

[
18
]

In light of the facts, the arguments advanced by
the parties, and the applicable law, the resolution of this appeal is
determined by answering the following questions:

(a)

Did the trial judge err in concluding that SIGA
had just cause to dismiss Mr. Thomas without notice?

(b)

Did the trial judge err in awarding costs to
SIGA on Column 2 of the Tariff?

IV.

ANALYSIS

A.

Did the trial judge err in concluding that SIGA
had just cause to dismiss Mr. Thomas without notice?

[
19
]

The trial judge found that SIGA had just cause
to dismiss Mr. Thomas without notice. Mr. Thomas asserts that, in reaching
that conclusion, the trial judge committed several errors, including:

(a)

finding that Mr. Thomas’ conduct in the October 10,
2018, meeting with Mr. Hryniuk amounted to insubordination;

(b)

finding that Mr. Thomas had breached the
anti-harassment and workplace violence policies without having made a determination
that Mr. Hryniuk’s fear of Mr. Thomas was reasonable;

(c)

finding that Mr. Thomas’ complaints about
perceived discrimination were a form of misconduct;

(d)

finding that a single act of misconduct was
sufficient to amount to just cause for dismissal; and

(e)

finding that Mr. Thomas had violated the
instruction not to contact other employees supported SIGA’s position, when the
instruction was neither lawful nor clear;

[
20
]

I will address each of these arguments in turn
but, before doing that, it may be useful to briefly review some of the legal
principles applicable to the question of dismissal for cause.

1.

Dismissal for cause – the governing legal
principles

[
21
]

The determination of whether an employee’s
alleged misconduct amounts to just cause for dismissal involves a contextual
analysis with an eye to proportionality (
McKinley v BC Tel
,

2001
SCC 38
, [2001] 2 SCR 161 [
McKinley
];
Balzer v Federated Co-operatives
Ltd.
,

2018 SKCA 93
at paras
19 and 50
, [2019] 1 WWR 411;
Retail,
Wholesale Department Store Union v Yorkton Cooperative Association
,

2017
SKCA 107
at paras
37 and 40
). The question to be addressed is whether, in the
circumstances, the behaviour of the employee was such that the employment
relationship could no longer viably exist (
McKinley

at para
29
). In
Dowling
v Ontario (Workplace Safety and Insurance Board)
(2004),
2004 CanLII 43692 (ON CA)
, 246 DLR (4th) 65
(Ont CA), Gillese J.A. summarized the principles emerging from
McKinley
as
follows:

[49]      Following

McKinley
, it can be seen that the core question for determination is
whether an employee has engaged in misconduct that is incompatible with the
fundamental terms of the employment relationship. The rationale for the
standard is that the sanction imposed for misconduct is to be proportional --
dismissal is warranted when the misconduct is sufficiently serious that it
strikes at the heart of the employment relationship. This is a factual inquiry
to be determined by a contextual examination of the nature and circumstances of
the misconduct.

[50]      Application
of the standard consists of:

1. determining the
nature and extent of the misconduct;

2. considering the
surrounding circumstances; and,

3. deciding
whether dismissal is warranted (i.e. whether dismissal is a proportional
response).

[
22
]

Whether misconduct amounts to just cause for
dismissal is a question of mixed fact and law

(
Lau v Royal Bank of
Canada
,

2017 BCCA 253
at para
35
;
Steel v Coast Capital Savings
Credit Union
,

2015 BCCA 127
at para
31
, 383 DLR (4th) 481). This
means the applicable standard of review is one of palpable and overriding
error, unless an extricable error of law or principle is identified (
Housen
v Nikolaisen
,

2002 SCC 33
at paras
36–37
, [2002] 2 SCR 235).

2.

The principles applied to Mr. Thomas’ arguments

[
23
]

Mr. Thomas’ first line of attack is that the
trial judge erred by finding, as he did in paragraphs 33 and 34 of the
Trial
Decision
,

that Mr. Thomas had been insubordinate to Mr. Hryniuk
during the October 10 meeting. Citing
Henry v Foxco Ltd.
,

2004
NBCA 22
at para
76
, 269 NBR (2d) 63 [
Henry
], he contends that
insubordination means “an employee’s intentional refusal to
obey an employer’s lawful and reasonable orders”. He argues that, while the
trial judge’s factual findings may have supported a conclusion that he was
insolent towards Mr. Hryniuk, they did not support a finding that he had been
insubordinate, because he had not disobeyed any lawful and reasonable orders
during the October 10 meeting. Mr. Thomas submits that this error provides a
basis for appellate intervention because insolence is generally seen as a less
serious form of misconduct than insubordination, and it was a legal error or an
error in principle for the trial judge to have conflated the two concepts.

[
24
]

I would not give effect to this argument. As I
will explain, even though the trial judge may have been incorrect to describe
Mr. Thomas’ conduct during the October 10 meeting as insubordination, when the
Trial
Decision
is read as a whole, it is apparent that this error had no impact
on the bottom-line result.

[
25
]

In its statement of defence, SIGA had pleaded
that Mr. Thomas’ conduct during the October 10 meeting amounted to “[h]arassment
and insubordination towards a supervisor”. However, when those pleadings are
read in light of all of the evidence, including the dismissal letter, it is
apparent that SIGA was really asserting that Mr. Thomas had been insolent. Insubordination
and insolence on the part of an employee are each capable, on their own, of
giving just cause for dismissal, and both are frequently used interchangeably (see,
generally, David Harris,
Wrongful Dismissal
, loose-leaf (Rel 10, October
2021) vol 1

(Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2021) at §5.54 [Harris]; and
Henry

at para
34
).
As I read
McKinley
,

the particular label attached to the category
of misconduct does not govern the determination. The requisite contextual
analysis calls for consideration of the degree of the misconduct that is said
to justify dismissal and an assessment of whether, having regard to all the
circumstances, it is of such a nature as to destroy the employment relationship.

[
26
]

In my view, the trial judge correctly instructed
himself on the law with respect to what amounts to just cause for dismissal.
Indeed, Mr. Thomas does not assert legal error with respect to the trial
judge’s identification of the applicable law. In the paragraphs that followed
the reference to insubordination, the trial judge’s reasons demonstrate that,
regardless of whether the proper label was applied to Mr. Thomas’ misconduct,
he kept his focus in the right place, namely, the seriousness of the misconduct
and its effect on the continuing viability of the employment relationship.

[
27
]

Mr. Thomas’ second argument is that the trial
judge erred by finding that he had breached SIGA’s Anti-Harassment and Workplace
Violence policy. The relevant portion of this policy reads as follows:

4. Policies

4.1 Harassment and
Workplace Violence

1. Policy

a. SIGA has zero
tolerance and is committed to providing a safe and healthy work environment
free from violence, threats of violence, harassment, intimidation and
disruptive behaviours for all our employees, contractors and patrons. SIGA
strictly prohibits harassment or violence that affects the workplace.

…

3. Employees

- Employees shall
not engage in the harassment of, or violence towards, any co-worker, contractor
or patron…

…

5. Definitions

5.1 Harassment

1. Harassment
means any inappropriate conduct, comment, display, action or gesture by a
person that constitutes a threat to the health or safety of a worker.

…

5.2 Workplace violence

1. The attempted,
threatened or actual conduct of a person that causes or is likely to cause
injury, and includes any threatening statement or behaviour that gives a worker
reasonable cause to believe that the worker is at risk of injury.

2. Incidents of
violence include:

a. Attempted or
actual assaults; and

b. Any threatening
statement or behaviour which gives the employee reasonable cause to believe
that he/she is at risk of injury

[
28
]

The basis for Mr. Thomas’ argument on this point
is that the trial judge found as a fact that, during the October 10 meeting, Mr.
Thomas had not uttered an explicit threat to Mr. Hryniuk, but only that “Mr.
Hryniuk felt threatened by Mr. Thomas” (
Trial Decision
at para 31). Mr.
Thomas points out that the trial judge accepted that Mr. Hryniuk “was hurt, and
that he felt threatened, and that he was fearful to the point of deferring his
departure from the SIGA building and deferring his arrival at his own home”
because of Mr. Thomas’ conduct in the meeting (at para 29), but no finding
was made about whether Mr. Hryniuk’s fear was reasonable, or whether it was
simply an overreaction. Mr. Thomas says that, in the absence of an explicit
threat, or a finding that Mr. Hryniuk had reasonable cause to believe that
he was at risk of injury, it was an error for the trial judge to have found
that he had breached the Anti-Harassment and Workplace Violence policy, because
his conduct did not meet the definition of workplace violence.

[
29
]

I would also not give effect to this argument,
in large measure because it is based on an improperly narrow reading of one
portion of the policy. This narrow reading ignores both the policy’s full
wording and the trial judge’s findings of fact. As set out above, the policy
clearly prohibits “harassment, intimidation and disruptive behaviours”. The
trial judge found that, during the October 10 meeting, Mr. Thomas had become angry
and aggressive with Mr. Hryniuk (including physically leaning toward him and
pointing his finger at him), had directed anger and resentment towards him, and
had elevated the tension in the room to the point that Mr. Hryniuk felt
threatened. He also found that Mr. Thomas had used profane language and belittled
Mr. Hryniuk on a point of fundamental significance to SIGA.

[
30
]

It is important to note here that the trial
judge did not rely solely on the evidence of Mr. Hryniuk in making those
findings; there was also the testimony of Mr. Bugler, which he explicitly
accepted. Mr. Bugler testified that, during the incident in question, he
briefly thought that Mr. Thomas “might take a swing” at Mr. Hryniuk. He also
said that, even though he had dealt with many angry employees during his
career, he had never before seen anything like what he observed in Mr. Thomas that
day. In the face of that evidence, I can see no error in the trial judge’s
conclusion that Mr. Thomas’ actions amounted to “disruptive behaviour towards
Mr. Hryniuk” that violated the Anti-Harassment and Workplace Violence policy (
Trial
Decision
at para 36(b)). In light of that conclusion, there was no need for
the trial judge to make a specific finding about whether Mr. Hryniuk reasonably
feared for his safety, so as to engage the definition of “workplace violence”
on that basis as well.

[
31
]

Mr. Thomas’ third argument is that the trial
judge effectively punished him for complaining to his supervisors about what he
perceived as discriminatory treatment. It was an error, says Mr. Thomas,
for the trial judge to have found this to be misconduct.

[
32
]

I reject this argument as well. As I read the
Trial
Decision
,

the trial judge did not find Mr. Thomas’ conduct
during the October 10 meeting to be problematic because he had raised a
complaint about perceived discrimination. The motivation for Mr. Thomas’
actions was not the issue; his actions and his conduct towards Mr. Hryniuk were
the problem. To put that another way, it was the
manner
in which Mr.
Thomas had gone about voicing his displeasure (which included profane language,
belittling comments and physically intimidating actions that caused his
supervisor to be fearful), that led to the finding of just cause, not the
subject
matter
that he had raised. I do not accept Mr. Thomas’ assertion that
upholding the trial judge’s reasoning would amount to a finding that employees
cannot raise legitimate concerns about discrimination without fear of giving
cause for dismissal. Regardless of the subject matter of a complaint, the manner
in which it is raised is a relevant and important component of the contextual
analysis when considering whether there is just cause for dismissal.

[
33
]

Mr. Thomas’ fourth argument zeroes in on the
fact that his conduct on October 10, 2018, was an isolated incident, which
ended when he left the meeting of is own accord, and that he had no prior
history of misconduct. He also notes that Mr. Hryniuk agreed that the incident
was very much out of character. In light of all this, Mr. Thomas asserts that
the trial judge erred by finding that a single act of misconduct was sufficient
to amount to cause for summary dismissal.

[
34
]

In particular, Mr. Thomas contends that the
trial judge failed to have proper regard for the relevant jurisprudence, citing

Gjema v Mercury Specialty Products Inc.
,
2012 MBQB 83
, 277 Man R (2d)
199;
Shakur v Mitchell Plastics
,

2012 ONSC 1008
; and
Phanlouvong
v Northfield Metal Products (1994) Ltd. et al
,

2014 ONSC 6585
, as
examples of decisions in which more egregious acts of workplace violence were
held to be insufficient to amount to cause for dismissal. I understand this to
be an assertion that the trial judge overlooked such important factors as the
relative lack of actual physical violence involved in Mr. Thomas’ outburst, and
SIGA’s failure to consider whether there were reasonable alternatives to
dismissal.

[
35
]

Once again, I do not find this argument
persuasive. In my view, it misses one of the central points of the decision in
McKinley
,

namely that, under the contextual analysis, the question of whether an
employee’s misconduct is sufficient to amount to cause for summary dismissal is
largely factual in nature. It is fair to say that in many – perhaps even most –
cases, a single incident of misconduct in the nature of insubordination or insolence
will be insufficient to justify immediate dismissal. But it would be incorrect
to say that a single incident of such misconduct can
never
justify
immediate dismissal. The determining factor is whether the nature of the
misconduct causes irreparable damage to the employment relationship. That
determination must be rooted in the particular facts of each case, as Robertson
J.A. observed in
Henry
:

[111]    A
review of the jurisprudence leads me to conclude that a single incident of
insolence

will justify summary dismissal of an employee in one of three circumstances:
(1) the employee and superior are no longer capable of maintaining a working
relationship; (2) the incident undermined the supervisor’s credibility in the
workplace and, correlatively, his or her ability to supervise effectively; or
(3) that because of the incident the employer suffered a material financial
loss, a loss of reputation or its business interests were seriously prejudiced.
I confess that these three possibilities do not constitute discrete tests to be
applied independently of one another. They may overlap and other exceptional
circumstances may exist: see generally Ellen E. Mole,
The Wrongful Dismissal
Handbook
(Toronto: Butterworths, 1997) at pp. 75-76.

[112]    The
impact of the misconduct on the working relationship between the two persons
involved in the verbal exchange is a necessary consideration. Depending on what
was said, the ability of the two employees to continue working together must be
addressed. As well, the impact that the confrontation had on other employees
who witnessed the incident is equally pertinent. A supervisor’s ability to
manage effectively can be undermined, if his or her credibility is destroyed in
front of other employees. Finally, the misconduct may be prejudicial to the
employer’s legitimate financial interests.

[113]    Admittedly,
the above framework is not entirely objective. An element of subjectivity
exists because of the need to draw inferences from primary findings of fact.
The decision-maker must draw his or her own inferences based on the totality of
the evidence. …

(Emphasis in original)

[
36
]

Harris also notes that a single violent outburst
by an employee, whether verbal, physical or both, against an employer or
supervisor “will frequently provide cause for summary dismissal”, because “[i]t
is obvious that such conduct carries a high risk of destruction of the
employment relationship” (at §5.55).

[
37
]

There are also several examples in the
jurisprudence of cases in which a single incident of insolence, not involving
physical violence, has been found to amount to cause for immediate dismissal. One
such example is
Bennett v Cunningham
(2006),

2006 CanLII 37516 (ON SC)
,
55 CCEL (3d) 304
(Ont Sup Ct [
Bennett
])
.
In that case the
plaintiff, a junior lawyer, was employed by a senior lawyer in a two-person
practice. The plaintiff sent a letter to the senior lawyer that was highly
critical of the way the office was run and questioned the senior lawyer’s integrity.
After being dismissed without notice, the plaintiff sued for wrongful
dismissal. The trial judge dismissed the action, finding that the employer had
just cause to terminate the plaintiff. In that respect, the trial judge
observed that “
a single incident of insolence will
justify summary dismissal if the employer and employee are no longer capable of
maintaining a working relationship” and that “the comments and accusations in
the letter undermined the confidence” that the employer had in the plaintiff
and “destroyed the employment relationship” (at paras 34 and 42). The Ontario Court
of Appeal ultimately upheld the trial decision, finding that “the trial judge’s
conclusion in this regard is essentially factual in nature, and, absent palpable
and overriding error, will not be overturned on appeal” (
Bennett v
Cunningham
,

2012 ONCA 540
,

at para
17
,
296 OAC 343
).

[
38
]

Another example is seen in
Wise v Broadway
Properties Ltd.
,

2005 BCCA 546
, 218 BCAC 204. In that case, the
plaintiff had worked for approximately 10 years as resident caretaker of an
apartment block. In a letter to his employer, he threatened to bring an action
against the employer to recover the value of work for which he believed he was
entitled to be paid, and compared himself to Jewish people who had been forced to
perform unpaid labour for various corporate entities in Germany during the
Second World War. The plaintiff’s principal, a Jewish man, was understandably
deeply offended by this. The plaintiff’s employment was terminated without
notice and he sued for wrongful dismissal. The trial judge dismissed the
action, finding that the insult in the letter had destroyed any chance of a
workable relationship between the plaintiff and his employer. The British
Columbia Court of Appeal upheld the trial decision, saying “[t]he trial judge’s
conclusion about the effect of the insult on the employment relationship is
bound up in his appreciation of the evidence and it is not palpably wrong. That
being so, we cannot interfere with the result” (at para 20).

[
39
]

In the present case, as set out above, the
trial judge drew several key conclusions about Mr. Thomas’ conduct. Most
pointedly, he found that Mr. Thomas’ conduct in the October 10, 2018, meeting
was of such a nature that the “employer-employee relationship could not
continue” because it “had been irretrievably severed” (
Trial Decision
at
para 34). The trial judge held that what Mr. Thomas had done in the meeting had
“destroyed both that fundamental trust and the capacity to work together” that
was pivotal to the employment relationship, and that it was “not realistic or
reasonable to think that any other person in a supervisory or management role
with SIGA could” work with him. Accordingly, the trial judge concluded that Mr.
Thomas’ misconduct “struck at the heart of the employment relationship” (at
paras 34–35). These were all factual findings and I see no palpable or
overriding error in any of them. As such, they are entitled to deference.

[
40
]

Moreover, I see no error in the trial judge’s application
of the law to his factual findings. He instructed himself properly with respect
to the governing law and applied the contextual approach in the way that
McKinley

directs
.
In short, there is no proper basis to interfere with his
conclusion on this point.

[
41
]

Mr. Thomas’ final argument is that the trial
judge erred by finding that he had committed misconduct by violating the
instruction not to contact other employees during the investigation, because
the instruction was neither lawful nor clear.

[
42
]

I would also not give effect to this argument. Even
if I were to assume, for the sake of argument, that the trial judge had erred
in this respect, such an error could not be said to have had an impact on the
bottom-line conclusion. The trial judge found that just cause for dismissal had
been established on the basis of Mr. Thomas’ conduct in the October 10, 2018,
meeting alone. Whether or not Mr. Thomas had violated SIGA’s instruction not to
communicate with other employees during the investigation had no bearing on
that determination.

[
43
]

In the result, I find no basis to interfere
with the trial judge’s conclusion that SIGA had just cause to terminate Mr.
Thomas’ employment without notice. That conclusion, as Mr. Thomas conceded
before this Court, also precludes any interference with the trial judge’s
determination regarding aggravated damages.

B.

Did the trial judge err in awarding costs to
SIGA on Column 2 of the tariff?

[
44
]

After dismissing Mr. Thomas’ claim, the trial
judge awarded costs to SIGA on column 2 of the Tariff of Costs. He gave no
explicit reasons for doing so. Mr. Thomas argues that the absence of reasons,
in and of itself, amounts to a legal error. He also suggests that neither the
length nor the complexity of the matter justified a departure from assessing
costs on Column 1.

[
45
]

I would reject this argument as well. Two
important points guide me to this result. The first is that costs awards are
inherently discretionary in nature and, as such, appellate courts will interfere
only where the judge who made the award “misapplied some governing principle or
rule or disregarded some critical fact or other consideration” or if the “costs
award is itself ‘so obviously unjust as to invite intervention’” (
Wongstedt
v Wongstedt
,

2017 SKCA 100
at para
41
, [2018] 4 WWR 82). The second
important point is that a lack of reasons for a costs award is not, standing
alone, a justification for appellate intervention (
K.R. v J.K.
,

2018
SKCA 35
at para
101
).

[
46
]

Rule 11-1 of
The Queen’s Bench Rules
speaks
to a judge’s discretion to award costs. The general rule is that the successful
party in an action is entitled to costs. Rule 11-1(3)(a) provides that the
court may “fix all or part of the costs with or without reference to the
Tariff”. Rule 11-1(4) lists a number of factors that the court may consider in
exercising its discretion as to costs. Among others, they include the result of
the proceedings, the amounts claimed and recovered, the importance of the
issues, the complexity of the proceedings, and the conduct of the parties
within the proceedings. As with the decision of whether to award costs, the
decision as to which column of the Tariff should be used involves an exercise
of discretion. In
1348623 Alberta Ltd. v Choubal
,

2016 SKQB 200
,
94 CPC (7th) 210, Danyliuk J. succinctly described the factors to be considered
in that respect:

[28]      There is no
“magic” rule to apply to determine costs. As stated in
Northland Material
Handling Inc. v Parkland (County)
,
2012 ABQB 586
at para
26
,

77 Alta LR
(5th) 150
: “Rather than one principle,
the weight of the case law establishes that the facts and circumstances of each
particular case must be assessed to determine whether a higher column or a
multiple of a column is appropriate in that case”. I agree.

…

[30]      Our
Queen’s
Bench Rules
list some factors to consider in deciding what cost award to
make. There is no corresponding list to determine which column of the tariff to
use once that cost order is made. The tariff itself clearly imports complexity
as the dominant consideration in selection of a column.

[31]      Distilling
the cases and considering the nature of our Rules and tariff, it strikes me
that in determining on which column party-and-party costs ought to be awarded,
the following factors should be considered:

(a)

Complexity
of the case.
…

(b)
Importance
of the case.
…

(c)
The
duration and conduct of the proceedings.
…

(d)
The urgency
of the matter.
…

(e)
The amount
at issue.
…

(f)
Whether
experts were involved.
…

(g)
Parity and
expectations.
…

(h)
Access to
justice.
…

(i)
Discretion
and reasonableness.
…

(j)
Any other
relevant matter.
…

(Emphasis in original)

[
47
]

In the present case, the issues cannot be
described as particularly complex and the amount of money at issue was not
large by contemporary litigation standards. That said, the case concerned a
matter of fundamental importance to both Mr. Thomas and SIGA. It also involved
a trial that lasted three days, during which each side called and examined
several witnesses and tendered documentary evidence. As SIGA points out,
comparable cases in which actions for wrongful dismissal have proceeded to
trial have resulted in costs awards on Column 2 (see, for example,
Kraus v
S3 Manufacturing Inc.
,

2020 SKQB 175
; and
Compton v Partners in
Motion Pictures Inc.
,

2005 SKQB 310
, 42 CCEL (3d) 35. Taking all of
that into account, I see no basis to conclude that the trial judge misapplied a
governing principle or that he disregarded a material fact or other material
consideration in the exercise of his discretion regarding costs. Nor am I
persuaded that the costs award is obviously unjust. Accordingly, deference is
warranted.

V.

CONCLUSION

[
48
]

For the foregoing reasons, the appeal is
dismissed. SIGA is entitled to the costs of the appeal, calculated in the usual
way.
